items.hint1: Start with the phrase 'a competitive good'. Ask what kind of relationship between two goods that phrase describes.
items.hint2: Competitive goods are substitutes: each can be used in place of the other, like two brands of bottled water. When one becomes dearer, buyers look at the other.
items.hint3: A rise in Y's own price cannot make people buy more Y. So the answer is about X. Decide whether buyers move towards X or away from it.
items.solution:
Answer: A. increase in quantity of X demanded

Competitive goods are substitutes, goods that can take each other's place. When the price of one rises, many buyers switch to the other, so more of the other is bought.

How to tell: the price of Y goes up, so Y becomes dearer compared with X. Buyers who used to buy Y move to X, and the quantity of X demanded rises. The phrase 'perfectly elastic' in the stem is loosely worded, but it does not change the direction of this effect.

Why not the others:
B. decrease in quantity of X demanded: this is what happens with complements (joint demand), goods used together, not with substitutes.
C. increase in quantity of Y demanded: by the law of demand, a rise in Y's own price reduces the quantity of Y demanded.
D. none of the above: A correctly describes the effect, so this cannot be chosen.

Exam tip: for related goods, first ask whether they are substitutes or complements. For substitutes, a price rise in one raises demand for the other. For complements, it lowers demand for the other.

items.hint1: Think about how most Nigerians earn their living, in villages as well as in towns.
items.hint2: 'Largest employer' means the sector with the most workers, not the one that pays best or grows fastest. Sport employs very few people.
items.hint3: Narrow it to the two sectors found in every village and town. Which of them gives work to people in a great many rural households?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Agricultural

Agriculture employs the largest share of Nigeria's workers. Many rural households farm, fish or rear animals, often on a small scale, and many more people work in trading, processing and moving farm produce.

How to tell: 'largest employer' asks about the number of people working in a sector. A large part of Nigeria's population lives in rural areas, and farming is the main work there.

Why not the others:
A. information technology: it is growing fast, but it employs a small share of workers, mostly in cities.
C. education: teachers and school staff are a much smaller group than farmers.
D. sport: very few people earn their living from sport.

Exam tip: 'largest employer' is about the number of workers, not income or growth. In questions about Nigeria and West Africa, agriculture is the sector the syllabus names as the largest employer.

items.hint1: An exchange rate links two currencies. When one gains value against the other, look at the same change from the other currency's side.
items.hint2: Inflation is about the general level of prices inside a country, not the exchange rate. And if the Naira has gained value, it has not lost value.
items.hint3: If each Naira now buys more Dollars, then each Dollar buys fewer Naira. Decide what that means for the Dollar, then see whether any option says it.
items.solution:
Answer: C. depreciation of Dollar

An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. If the Naira rises in value against the Dollar (the Naira appreciates), each Dollar now buys fewer Naira, so the Dollar has fallen in value against the Naira (the Dollar depreciates).

How to tell: suppose $1 = ₦1,500 changes to $1 = ₦1,200. Each Naira is now worth more, so the Naira has appreciated. Each Dollar now buys only ₦1,200 instead of ₦1,500, so the Dollar has depreciated against the Naira. The expected phrase 'appreciation of Naira' is not offered, but C describes the same change from the Dollar's side.

Why not the others:
A. inflation: that is a general rise in prices inside a country, not a change in the exchange rate.
B. depreciation of Naira: that would mean the Naira losing value, the opposite of what the stem says.
D. none of the above: C correctly describes the same event, so this does not fit.

Exam tip: an exchange rate has two sides. When one currency appreciates against another, the other depreciates against it. If the option you expect is missing, look for its mirror image.

items.hint1: Depreciation makes imported goods dearer in Naira. Think about what must happen next for local industry to benefit.
items.hint2: Local industry gains when buyers respond to dearer imports by buying fewer of them and more locally made goods.
items.hint3: Compare the size of the depreciation with how buyers react to it. Picture imports becoming much dearer while people keep buying just as much. Which factor decided the outcome?
items.solution:
Answer: D. The elasticity of demand for imported product

Depreciation lowers the value of the Naira, so imports cost more in Naira. This protects local industry when buyers respond by buying fewer imports and more local goods, that is, when demand for imports is elastic (responsive to price).

How to tell: if demand for imports is elastic, a rise in their price causes a large fall in the quantity bought, and buyers turn to local products. If demand is inelastic, as with essential goods that have no local substitute, people keep buying imports at the higher price, and local industry gains little.

Why not the others:
A. government policies: policy can cause the depreciation, but it does not decide how buyers react to dearer imports.
B. the degree of depreciation: even a large depreciation achieves little if import demand is inelastic.
C. the period of depreciation: how long it lasts matters less than whether buyers respond to the higher prices.

Exam tip: whenever a question asks what makes devaluation or depreciation work, think of the elasticity of demand for imports and exports. The policy works best when demand is elastic.

items.hint1: Food production depends on land, tools, money and, above all, people to do the farm work. Look for the option that takes something away from farming.
items.hint2: A subsidy is help from government that lowers a farmer's costs. An agro-processing company buys farm produce to turn into other products. Ask what each of these does to a farmer's reason to produce.
items.hint3: Test each option by asking whether it adds to or takes away from what farmers need. Pay close attention to what happens to the number of people working on farms.
items.solution:
Answer: A. Rural migration

Food production in Nigeria depends heavily on human labour, because much of the farming is done by hand on small farms. Rural-urban migration, the movement of people from villages to towns, takes this labour away, so less food is produced.

How to tell: when young people leave the villages for city jobs, the farmers left behind have fewer hands for clearing, planting and harvesting. Farms shrink or are abandoned. The other three options add to what farmers have or can earn.

Why not the others:
B. development of agro-processing company: these firms buy farm produce as raw material, which gives farmers a ready market and a reason to grow more.
C. social in infrastructure in rural areas: roads, water, power and clinics in rural areas make farming easier and encourage people to stay.
D. subsiding farmer: this means subsidising farmers, which lowers their costs of seeds, fertiliser and tools and so raises output.

Exam tip: in problems-of-agriculture questions, rural-urban migration is a standard cause of low output because it drains farm labour. Anything that gives farmers markets, money or services is a remedy, not a problem.

items.hint1: Recall the definition of dumping in international trade. It compares the price of the same good in two different markets.
items.hint2: Dumping is about selling abroad cheaply. Equal prices in the two markets would be ordinary trade, not dumping.
items.hint3: In the stem, 'local price' means the price in the exporter's home country. Decide which of the two markets gets the lower price, then compare.
items.solution:
Answer: B. higher

Dumping is selling a good in a foreign market at a price lower than the price charged for it in the producer's home market, sometimes even below its cost. Firms do it to get rid of surplus stock or to win a foreign market.

How to tell: the stem compares the local (home) price with the foreign price. Under dumping the foreign price is the low one, so the local price is higher than the foreign price.

Why not the others:
A. lower: this reverses the definition, because under dumping the foreign buyer gets the cheaper price.
C. equal: equal prices in both markets would be ordinary trade, not dumping.
D. none of the above: B fits the definition, so this cannot be chosen.

Exam tip: in dumping questions, first fix which market is 'home' and which is 'foreign'. Dumping means the foreign market gets the lower price, which is why importing countries use anti-dumping duties to protect their own producers.

items.hint1: In an odd-one-out question, find what three of the options have in common. Here, think about the different ways a company raises money.
items.hint2: Some sources of funds are securities: papers a company issues to the public, which people can buy and sell on the stock exchange.
items.hint3: Ask of each option: does the company issue it to the public, and can it be traded on the capital market? The odd one fails that test.
items.solution:
Answer: C. Bank loan

Ordinary shares, preference shares and debentures are all securities. A company issues them to the public to raise long-term capital, and they can be bought and sold on the stock exchange. A bank loan is borrowing from one lender under a private agreement, so it is not a security.

How to tell: ordinary and preference shareholders buy part-ownership of the company. Debenture holders lend money to the company and receive fixed interest. In all three cases the holder has a paper that can be traded on the capital market. A bank loan gives no such tradable paper.

Why not the others:
A. preference share: a security issued by a company, paying a fixed dividend.
B. debentures: a security issued by a company, a long-term loan from the public that pays fixed interest.
D. Ordinary shares: a security issued by a company, giving ownership and a share of the profits.

Exam tip: in odd-one-out questions, look for a grouping that puts three options together and leaves exactly one out. A grouping that splits the options two and two, such as owners against lenders, is not the one the examiner wants.

items.hint1: Start from what deficit financing means: the government spends more than it collects in revenue. Think about what that extra spending does to total demand in the economy.
items.hint2: The gap is often filled by borrowing, especially from the central bank, or by creating new money. Either way, more money comes into the economy.
items.hint3: If more money is spent on roughly the same quantity of goods, does the general price level tend to rise or fall?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Inflationary

Deficit financing means the government spends more than its revenue and covers the gap by borrowing or by creating new money. The extra spending raises total demand in the economy. If output does not rise as fast, prices tend to go up.

How to tell: deficit spending adds money and demand to the economy. In the syllabus this is treated as a cause of demand-pull inflation, especially when the deficit is financed by the central bank.

Why not the others:
A. deflationary: deflation is a fall in the general price level, but deficit financing adds to demand rather than reducing it.
C. De-inflationary: this means bringing inflation down, which comes from cutting spending or raising taxes, the opposite of a deficit.
D. neutral: extra government spending changes total demand, so its effect on prices is not neutral.

Exam tip: link each budget type to its effect on prices. A deficit budget adds to demand and is inflationary. A surplus budget takes money out of the economy and is used to fight inflation.

items.hint1: The question is about a consumer and satisfaction, not a producer and output. Recall the curves used in the theory of consumer behaviour.
items.hint2: A curve about inputs and output belongs to production, and a curve about what a whole economy can produce belongs to resource use. Neither measures a consumer's satisfaction.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, only one is drawn with a quantity of a different good on each axis. Which is it?
items.solution:
Answer: C. indifference

An indifference curve joins all the combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction. The consumer is 'indifferent' between any two points on it, because each gives equal satisfaction.

How to tell: the stem names two things: combinations of commodities, and the same satisfaction for a consumer. The indifference curve has a quantity of one good on each axis and equal satisfaction all along its length.

Why not the others:
A. isoquant: it shows combinations of inputs that give the same output for a producer, not satisfaction for a consumer.
B. demand curve: it shows the quantity of one good bought at different prices.
D. PPF: the production possibility frontier shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources, not what satisfies a consumer.

Exam tip: match the curve to who and what. Consumer plus equal satisfaction means indifference curve. Producer plus equal output means isoquant. Whole economy plus maximum output means PPF.

items.hint1: The question is about a producer combining inputs, such as labour and capital, to make output. Recall the curves used in the theory of production.
items.hint2: An indifference curve is about a consumer's satisfaction, so it does not fit a question about inputs and output.
items.hint3: Narrow it to the curves drawn for a single firm. Of those, which one has an input on each axis, rather than output on the vertical axis?
items.solution:
Answer: B. isoquant curve

An isoquant joins all the combinations of two inputs, such as labour and capital, that produce the same quantity of output. 'Iso' means equal and 'quant' is short for quantity, so the name itself says equal quantity.

How to tell: the stem names inputs and the same level of output. That is the producer's version of the indifference curve, and it is called an isoquant.

Why not the others:
A. PPF: it shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources, not combinations of inputs.
C. indifference curve: it shows combinations of goods giving a consumer equal satisfaction, not equal output.
D. MP curve: it shows the extra output from each extra unit of one input, not combinations of two inputs.

Exam tip: 'iso' means equal. Isoquant means equal output, isocost means equal cost. If the stem says inputs giving the same output, choose the isoquant.

items.hint1: Recall what marginal product measures: the change in total product when one more unit of the variable input, such as one more worker, is added.
items.hint2: Marginal product rises in the early stage and falls later, but both of those happen while total product is still growing, before it reaches its peak.
items.hint3: At the very top of the total product curve, total product is neither going up nor coming down. Decide whether one more worker adds a steady amount there, or nothing at all.
items.solution:
Answer: D. zero

Marginal product (MP) is the extra output from one more unit of the variable input. Total product (TP) keeps rising while MP is positive and starts to fall once MP becomes negative. So at the point where TP is at its maximum, MP is zero.

How to tell:
Suppose 5 workers produce 40 bags and 6 workers also produce 40 bags.
TP has reached its peak of 40 bags.
MP of the 6th worker = 40 − 40 = 0 bags.
A 7th worker would make TP fall, giving a negative MP.

Why not the others:
A. falling: MP falls on the way up to the peak, but at the peak itself it has fallen all the way to zero.
B. Rising: MP rises in the early stage, when TP is increasing faster and faster, well before the peak.
C. constant: a constant positive MP would mean TP was still rising, so it could not be at its maximum.

Exam tip: link the curves. When MP is positive, TP rises. When MP is zero, TP is at its maximum. When MP is negative, TP falls.

items.hint1: In economics, the short run and the long run are not measured in months or years. They are defined by what the firm is able to change.
items.hint2: A fixed number of years cannot define the short run, because the time needed to change things differs from one industry to another.
items.hint3: Think of a bakery that can hire more bakers this week but cannot build a bigger oven room until next year. Which option describes the bakery's position this week?
items.solution:
Answer: C. time were fixed and variable inputs are combined

The short run is the period in which at least one input, such as land, buildings or machinery, is fixed, while other inputs, such as labour and raw materials, can be changed. The firm produces by combining its fixed inputs with more or less of the variable inputs.

How to tell: the short run is defined by what the firm can change, not by a length of time. A bakery can hire more bakers quickly, but it needs much longer to build a bigger oven room. Until it can do that, it is in the short run. In the long run, all inputs can be changed.

Why not the others:
A. 5 years: the short run is not a fixed number of years. It may be weeks for a small shop and years for a steel plant.
B. time: this is too vague to define anything, since every period is a period of time.
D. time when all of us are alive: this has nothing to do with how a firm uses its inputs.

Exam tip: short run means at least one input is fixed. Long run means all inputs can be varied. Reject any option that defines either one by a set number of years.

items.hint1: Good money has several qualities. The stem asks for the one that matters most, so ask which quality money cannot do without.
items.hint2: The stem asks for one feature, so an option that lumps several together does not answer 'most important'.
items.hint3: Imagine a coin that lasts for years and is easy to recognise, but traders refuse to take it. Can it still work as money?
items.solution:
Answer: C. acceptability

Economics texts name general acceptability as the most important feature of money. Something works as money because people are willing to take it in exchange for goods and services. Without that, it cannot act as a medium of exchange, however well it is made.

How to tell: durability and recognizability make money better, but they are of no use if sellers refuse it. Acceptability is the feature the other functions of money depend on.

Why not the others:
A. durability: lasting a long time is a good quality, but a durable item nobody accepts is not money.
B. recognizability: being easy to identify helps, but it does not make people accept something.
D. all of the above: the stem asks for the single most important feature, so a list of all of them does not fit.

Exam tip: when a question asks for the most important quality of money, choose general acceptability. It is what lets money serve as a medium of exchange.

items.hint1: Look first at the line labelled x, the demand or price line the firm faces. Notice its shape before you look at the other curves.
items.hint2: A firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve can raise its price and still sell some output. A firm facing a flat line cannot: it must accept the market price and can only choose how much to sell.
items.hint3: Ask how many sellers a market must have for one firm's demand line to be completely flat. Which option describes the market with the most sellers?
items.solution:
Answer: C. a perfect competitive market

In perfect competition there are very many firms selling the same product, so each firm is a price taker. It can sell as much as it wants at the market price, so its demand curve is a horizontal line on which price = average revenue (AR) = marginal revenue (MR).

How to tell: the line x is horizontal, so the firm faces one fixed price whatever quantity it sells. The two curves rising towards Y are the cost curves, the U-shaped average cost (AC) curve and the marginal cost (MC) curve, and they meet the price line at e, where the firm settles. A flat demand line is the mark of a perfectly competitive firm.

Why not the others:
A. a monopolistic market: a monopolist, or a firm in monopolistic competition, has some control over its price and faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
B. an oligopolistic market: each of the few large firms faces a downward-sloping demand curve and reacts to the others' prices.
D. a duopolistic market: with only two sellers, each firm can affect the price, so its demand curve slopes downward.

Exam tip: on a firm's cost and revenue diagram, check the demand (AR) line first. Horizontal means perfect competition. Downward-sloping means some form of imperfect competition.

items.hint1: The shaded rectangle runs from the origin up to the price line x and across to the output at e. The area of a rectangle is height × width, so ask what the height and the width stand for.
items.hint2: The height is the price and the width is the quantity sold, so the area is price × quantity. Marginal cost is shown by a curve on the diagram, not by an area.
items.hint3: Look at where the U-shaped average cost curve is at output e. If average cost equals price there, is there any gap left between price and average cost to show profit or loss? What does average cost × quantity give?
items.solution:
Answer: D. total cost

Total revenue is price × quantity, and total cost is average cost (AC) × quantity. When the AC curve meets the price line at the output chosen, these two are the same rectangle, so the firm just covers its costs and earns only normal profit.

How to tell:
Height of the shaded area = price, the level of line x.
Width of the shaded area = the output at e, marked by the dashed line.
At e, the AC curve passes through the price line, so AC = price.
Shaded area = price × output = AC × output = total cost.
The same area is also total revenue, but that is not one of the options.

Why not the others:
A. loss: a loss area would be a gap between a higher AC and a lower price, and there is no such gap at e.
B. profit: a supernormal profit area would be the gap between the price and a lower AC. Here AC equals price at e, so the firm earns only normal profit, which economists count as part of cost.
C. marginal cost: marginal cost is shown by a curve, not by an area on the diagram.

Exam tip: on a cost and revenue diagram, price × quantity is total revenue and AC × quantity is total cost. Profit or loss is the gap between those two rectangles, between the price line and the AC curve.

items.hint1: A schedule is a table. Think about which two things a demand table lists side by side.
items.hint2: An 'all of the above' option is right only if every other option is correct. Check whether 'various levels' actually says levels of what.
items.hint3: Recall the law of demand: as one thing rises, the quantity demanded falls. Which option names that thing?
items.solution:
Answer: C. quantity demanded at various price

A demand schedule is a table showing the quantities of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at various prices, over a given period. It is the table form of the demand curve.

How to tell: a demand schedule has two columns, price and quantity demanded. For example, at ₦100, 50 units; at ₦80, 70 units; at ₦60, 90 units. Price is the variable that changes down the table.

Why not the others:
A. quantity demanded at various time: the schedule covers one given period and lists different prices, not different times.
B. quantity demanded at various levels: this does not say levels of what, so it is not a definition.
D. all of the above: A and B are wrong, so this cannot be right.

Exam tip: questions on demand and supply schedules turn on price. If an option leaves out price, it is not the definition.

items.hint1: Recall the law of supply: how sellers respond when the price of their good changes.
items.hint2: When the price of a good rises, think about what producers want to do with the amount they offer for sale. 'Neutral' would mean price has no effect at all.
items.hint3: Two of the options mean the same thing, so they cannot both be right. Decide whether price and quantity supplied move in the same direction or in opposite directions.
items.solution:
Answer: A. positive

The law of supply states that, other things being equal, the higher the price, the greater the quantity supplied. Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, which is a positive (direct) relationship. Producers offer more at higher prices because it is more profitable.

How to tell: a supply schedule might read ₦50 → 20 units, ₦100 → 40 units, ₦150 → 60 units. As price rises, quantity supplied rises. That is why the supply curve slopes upward from left to right.

Why not the others:
B. negative: this is the relationship in a demand schedule, where quantity falls as price rises.
C. indirect: this means the same as negative, and it also describes demand.
D. neutral: this would mean price has no effect on quantity supplied, which goes against the law of supply.

Exam tip: demand has a negative (inverse) link between price and quantity, and supply has a positive (direct) link. If two options mean the same thing, as negative and indirect do here, neither is likely to be the answer.

items.hint1: Think about how national income is measured: it adds up goods and services that are sold for money and recorded.
items.hint2: Unpaid services, such as a parent cooking at home or a relative helping in the family shop without pay, produce real value but have no price attached, so they are not counted.
items.hint3: If real output is left out of the count, is the recorded figure bigger or smaller than the true value? Notice which options mean the same thing.
items.solution:
Answer: C. underestimate

National income is measured by adding up the market value of goods and services. Unpaid services, such as housework or caring for relatives, add real value but are not sold, so they are left out. Leaving out real output makes the recorded national income lower than the true figure.

How to tell: if a parent cooks, cleans and cares for children at home, that work is not recorded. If the family paid someone to do the same work, it would be counted. The work is the same, but only the paid version enters national income, so leaving out unpaid work makes the total too small.

Why not the others:
A. inflate: to inflate is to make bigger, but leaving something out makes the figure smaller.
B. overestimate: this also means the figure is too big, the opposite of what leaving something out does.
D. neutralize: leaving out real output does change the figure, so the effect is not neutral.

Exam tip: real output left out of national income, such as unpaid services or food grown for the family's own use, makes national income underestimated. Double counting, which counts the same output twice, makes it overestimated.

items.hint1: Of the three averages, mean, median and mode, the mode is found by counting, not by adding or by putting values in order.
items.hint2: Go through the list and count how many times each value appears. There are 15 values in all, so your counts should add up to 15.
items.hint3: Compare your counts for the two or three most common values. The mode is the value with the highest count, not the largest value.
items.solution:
Answer: D. 1

The mode is the value that occurs most often in a set of data. It is found by counting how many times each value appears.

How to tell:
Count each value in 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 0, 3, 5, 2, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 1:
0 appears 3 times
1 appears 6 times
2 appears 3 times
3 appears 2 times
5 appears 1 time
Check: 3 + 6 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 values
1 appears most often, so the mode is 1.

Why not the others:
A. 0: it appears 3 times, fewer than 1.
B. 3: it appears only 2 times.
C. 2: it appears 3 times, fewer than 1.

Exam tip: for the mode, make a quick tally of each value and check that the counts add up to the number of values. The mode is the value with the highest count, not the largest value.

items.hint1: The mean is the ordinary average: add all the values and divide by how many values there are.
items.hint2: There are 15 values. To add them quickly, count how many times each value appears and multiply each value by its count, then add the results.
items.hint3: Divide your total by 15 and round to two decimal places. If none of the options matches, add the values again, since one slip changes the answer.
items.solution:
Answer: C. 1.53

The arithmetic mean is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values. It uses every value in the data, so each one must be counted exactly once.

How to tell:
Number of values: n = 15
Multiply each value by how often it appears:
0 × 3 = 0
1 × 6 = 6
2 × 3 = 6
3 × 2 = 6
5 × 1 = 5
Sum = 0 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 5 = 23
Mean = 23 ÷ 15 = 1.533…, which is 1.53 to two decimal places.

Why not the others:
A. 1: this is the value that appears most often, not the average of all the values.
B. 2: this is the mean rounded to the nearest whole number, not the mean itself.
D. 5: this is the largest value in the data, not the average.

Exam tip: before calculating a mean, multiply each value by how often it appears, then divide by the total number of values. Check your mean is sensible: it must lie between the smallest and the largest values.

items.hint1: The median is the middle value once the data are arranged in order of size.
items.hint2: Arrange all 15 values from smallest to largest. With an odd number of values, the median is one single value in the middle, not an average of two.
items.hint3: With 15 values, there are 7 values on each side of the middle. Count along your ordered list to the 8th value.
items.solution:
Answer: B. 1

The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order. For n values, it is the value in position (n + 1) ÷ 2.

How to tell:
Ordered data: 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5
n = 15
Position = (15 + 1) ÷ 2 = 8th value
The 8th value is 1, so the median is 1.

Why not the others:
A. 0: 0 fills only positions 1 to 3, before the middle.
C. 2: 2 fills positions 10 to 12, after the middle.
D. 3: 3 fills positions 13 and 14, near the end of the list.

Exam tip: for the median, first arrange the data in order, then use (n + 1) ÷ 2 to find the middle position. Taking the middle of the unordered list is the commonest mistake.

items.hint1: The range is a measure of spread: it tells you how far apart the values in a set of data are.
items.hint2: Range = largest value − smallest value.
items.hint3: Scan the whole list for the very smallest and the very largest values, including any zeros, then subtract.
items.solution:
Answer: A. 5

The range is the simplest measure of dispersion (spread). It is the difference between the largest and the smallest values in the data.

How to tell:
Largest value = 5
Smallest value = 0
Range = 5 − 0 = 5

Why not the others:
B. 4: this comes from taking 1 as the smallest value, but the data contain 0.
C. 3: this would need the largest value to be 3, but 5 appears in the data.
D. 2: this is far smaller than the gap between the smallest and largest values.

Exam tip: for the range, find the two extreme values and subtract. Watch for zeros: 0 is a value in the data, and it is often the smallest.

items.hint1: A census is a full count of a country's population. It is costly and huge, so it is not done every year. Think about the usual gap between one count and the next.
items.hint2: Twenty years is too long, because the figures would be badly out of date for planning. Fifteen years is not a standard interval either.
items.hint3: Of the two left, think of the round number many countries use, so that each census falls in a year ending in the same digit.
items.solution:
Answer: B. 10

A population census is a count of every person in a country, with details such as age, sex and occupation. Following United Nations advice, most countries hold one about once every ten years, because it is very costly to organise and the figures stay useful for planning for about that long.

How to tell: the stem says 'usually', so it asks for the standard interval, not what one particular country does. The standard interval is ten years.

Why not the others:
A. 5: a few countries do count every five years, but ten years is the usual interval.
C. 15: this is longer than the standard interval.
D. 20: census figures would be far out of date for planning by then.

Exam tip: learn the standard census interval, ten years, and why a census matters: planning, revenue allocation and fixing constituencies. Note when a question asks what is usual rather than what every country achieves.

items.hint1: In odd-one-out questions, find what three of the names have in common. Think about what each person is known for.
items.hint2: J.M. Keynes is the economist known for ideas on government spending and unemployment. Check whether each of the other names also belongs to an economist.
items.hint3: One of the names belongs to an Italian mathematician of the 1400s whose book first set out the double-entry system of keeping business records. Which name is that?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Luca Paciolo

Luca Pacioli (spelt Paciolo in the question) was an Italian mathematician of the 1400s. He is called the father of accounting because his book of 1494 first set out double-entry bookkeeping. The other three are economists.

How to tell: J.S. Mill, J.M. Keynes and David Ricardo all wrote about how economies work, so they form the group. Pacioli wrote about recording business accounts, which is accounting, not economics.

Why not the others:
B. J.S Mill: John Stuart Mill was a classical economist who wrote Principles of Political Economy.
C. J.M Keynes: John Maynard Keynes was the economist who argued that government spending can reduce unemployment.
D. D. Richard: this is almost certainly David Ricardo, misspelt, the classical economist known for the theory of comparative advantage.

Exam tip: learn one idea for each major economist: Adam Smith and division of labour, Ricardo and comparative advantage, Malthus and population, Keynes and government spending. In odd-one-out questions on names, the odd name often comes from another field.

items.hint1: A regional organisation brings together countries from one part of the world. Ask where the members of each body come from.
items.hint2: The AU brings together African countries, and ECOWAS brings together West African countries.
items.hint3: Of the two left, one is made up of countries from one continent and the other takes members from every continent. Which one is not regional?
items.solution:
Answer: D. UN

A regional organisation has members from one region of the world. The United Nations (UN) has members from every continent, nearly every country in the world, so it is a global organisation, not a regional one.

How to tell: check the members. The AU is for African countries, the EU for European countries and ECOWAS for West African countries. The UN is open to countries everywhere.

Why not the others:
A. AU: the African Union brings together the countries of Africa.
B. EU: the European Union brings together countries in Europe.
C. ECOWAS: the Economic Community of West African States brings together countries in West Africa.

Exam tip: if a body's name contains a place, such as Africa, Europe or West Africa, it is usually regional. Bodies such as the UN, IMF, World Bank and WTO are global.

items.hint1: First sort the options into fiscal tools, which the government uses through its own spending and taxing, and monetary tools, which the central bank uses to control money and credit.
items.hint2: Interest rates and the money supply are controlled by the Central Bank of Nigeria, so they are monetary tools, not fiscal ones.
items.hint3: Of the two fiscal options left, one is a single source of revenue and the other is the plan that brings revenue, spending and borrowing together. Which is the broader tool?
items.solution:
Answer: A. budget

Fiscal policy is the use of government revenue and spending to guide the economy. In Nigerian economics texts, the budget is named as the main instrument of fiscal policy, because it brings taxation, spending and borrowing together in one plan for the year.

How to tell: first remove the monetary tools, interest rate and money supply, which the central bank controls. That leaves budget and taxes. Taxes are one part of the budget, while the budget covers taxes and spending together, so it is the broader and stronger tool.

Why not the others:
B. taxes: taxation is an important fiscal tool, but it is only the revenue side of the budget.
C. interest rate: this is a monetary tool set by the central bank, not a fiscal tool.
D. money supply: this is also controlled by the central bank, so it is a monetary tool.

Exam tip: government spending, taxation and the budget are fiscal. Interest rates, money supply, reserve requirements and open market operations are monetary. When asked for the main fiscal tool, choose the one that covers the others.

items.hint1: A maximum price is a legal upper limit: sellers may not charge more than it. Think about where it must be placed to make any difference to the market.
items.hint2: A price limit has an effect when it stops the market from settling at its own equilibrium price, the price where demand equals supply.
items.hint3: Suppose the equilibrium price of rice is ₦1,000 a kg. Would a law saying 'not more than ₦1,200' change anything? Now compare a limit of ₦800.
items.solution:
Answer: B. below the equilibrium

Maximum price legislation (a price ceiling) is a law that stops sellers charging more than a set price. Governments use it to keep essential goods affordable. It has an effect only when it is set below the equilibrium price, the price the market would reach on its own.

How to tell: if the equilibrium price of rice is ₦1,000 a kg, a maximum of ₦1,200 changes nothing, because sellers already charge ₦1,000. A maximum of ₦800 forces the price down. At that lower price more is demanded and less is supplied, so shortages, queues and black markets tend to follow.

Why not the others:
A. above the equilibrium: the market price is already below the limit, so the law would have no effect.
C. equal the equilibrium: the market would settle at that price anyway, so the law would change nothing.
D. hone of the above: B describes where a maximum price is set, so this cannot be chosen.

Exam tip: a maximum price is set below equilibrium and causes shortages. A minimum price is set above equilibrium and causes surpluses. Link each one to its effect.

items.hint1: The Central Bank of Nigeria is headed by a governor, a different office from the President and the Minister of Finance. Think about who held that post when this 2024 paper was set.
items.hint2: Bola Tinubu became President of Nigeria in 2023, and Wale Edun is the Minister of Finance. Neither of them runs the Central Bank.
items.hint3: Of the two names left, one looks like the name of the governor who left office in 2023. Which one was appointed to replace him?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Yemi Cardoso

The Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) heads the bank that controls money and banking in the country. Olayemi (Yemi) Cardoso was appointed CBN Governor in September 2023, so he held the post when the 2024 paper was set.

How to tell: separate the offices. The President leads the government, the Minister of Finance manages the government's finances, and the CBN Governor runs the central bank. In 2024 that third office was held by Cardoso.

Why not the others:
A. Bola Hammed Tinubu: he is the President of Nigeria, not the CBN Governor.
B. Wale Edun: he is the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, not the CBN Governor.
C. John Emetiole: this looks like a misspelling of Godwin Emefiele, the governor before Cardoso, who left office in 2023.

Exam tip: for 'current office holder' questions, the answer is the person in office when the paper was set. Know the President, the Minister of Finance and the CBN Governor, and keep their roles apart.

items.hint1: The Bank of Industry is a federal development bank that gives long-term loans to manufacturers and other businesses. Recall where its head office is.
items.hint2: The bank was formed in 2001 from older development banks, including the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank, which was set up in the 1960s and run from the country's capital of that time.
items.hint3: Narrow it to Nigeria's present capital and its old capital. Many federal agencies moved to the new capital, but some older banks kept their head office where they began.
items.solution:
Answer: B. Lagos

The Bank of Industry (BOI) is Nigeria's main development bank for industry. It gives long-term loans and support to manufacturers and small businesses. Its head office is at Marina, Lagos, where the older development banks it grew out of were based.

How to tell: BOI was formed in 2001 from older banks, including the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank. These were set up when Lagos was Nigeria's capital and business centre, and BOI kept its head office there. It has other offices around the country, including one in Abuja.

Why not the others:
A. Abuja: many federal agencies are based there, and BOI has an office there, but its head office is in Lagos.
C. Ogun: this is a state, and BOI's head office is not there.
D. Kano: this is a major commercial city in the north, but BOI's head office is not there.

Exam tip: do not assume every federal body has its head office in Abuja. The CBN is headquartered in Abuja, but some older financial institutions, such as the Bank of Industry, are run from Lagos.

items.hint1: This question asks for the relationship that is wrong, so three of the four are true. First decide where each lettered point sits on the graph: inside the curve, on it, or beyond it.
items.hint2: On this graph, a point further out from the corner where the two axes meet stands for more output. A point inside the curve stands for less output than a point on it. Two points on the same curve are treated as equal, even though they are different mixes of M and N.
items.hint3: Test each relationship against the picture. Be most careful with the ones that involve the point lying outside the curve: does that point stand for more or less output than the point it is compared with?
items.solution:
Answer: A. A>D

On a production possibility curve (PPC), where a point sits shows how much output it stands for. A point inside the curve means less than the country can make, a point on the curve means the most it can make with its present resources, and a point beyond the curve means more than it can make now.

How to tell: D lies beyond the curve. It has about the same amount of M as A but more of N, so D stands for more output than A, not less. The statement A>D says the opposite, so it is the wrong relationship.

Why not the others:
B. A=B: true, because A and B both lie on the curve, so they are equally efficient, even though they are different mixes of M and N.
C. A>C: true, because C lies inside the curve and has less M than A with about the same N.
D. C<D: true, because C is inside the curve and D is beyond it.

Exam tip: in 'which is wrong' questions on a PPC, rank the points first. Beyond the curve is highest, on the curve comes next (points on the curve rank equal), and inside the curve is lowest. Then look for the option that breaks that order.

items.hint1: Optimum here means the best a country can do with the resources it has now. Think about what each position on a production possibility curve, inside, on or beyond it, says about how resources are being used.
items.hint2: A point inside the curve means some workers, land or machines are idle or wasted. A point beyond the curve asks for more than the country can produce with what it has today, so it cannot be where the country is now.
items.hint3: Once you have ruled out the point that wastes resources and the point that cannot be reached, look at the options carefully: is there only one point on the curve itself, or more than one?
items.solution:
Answer: C. A and B

A country is at its optimum when it uses all its resources fully and efficiently. On a PPC, every point on the curve itself shows this, so there is a whole line of optimum points, not just one. Which of them the country picks depends on the mix of goods it wants.

How to tell: A and B both lie on the curve, so both show full and efficient use of resources. C lies inside the curve, so some resources are idle. D lies beyond the curve, so the country cannot produce it with what it has now.

Why not the others:
A. A: A is an optimum point, but B is on the curve too, so A alone is incomplete.
B. B: B is an optimum point, but A is on the curve too, so B alone is incomplete.
D. D: it lies beyond the curve, so the country cannot reach it with its present resources.

Exam tip: on a PPC, the words optimum, efficient and full employment of resources all point to the curve itself. If two points sit on the curve, look for the option that names both.

items.hint1: Reaching a point beyond the curve means the whole curve has to move outward. Ask what lets a country produce more of both goods, not just more of one of them.
items.hint2: The curve moves outward when the country's ability to produce grows: more or better resources, or better ways of using them. Choosing to produce less, or moving resources from one good to the other, does not change that ability.
items.hint3: Two options are left. For each one, ask: does this, on its own, raise how much the country can make from the workers, land and machines it has?
items.solution:
Answer: C. technological advancement

The PPC shows the most a country can produce with its present resources and methods. For the curve to move outward, so that a point like D sits on the new curve, the country's ability to produce must grow. Better technology does this: the same workers, land and machines can then make more of both goods.

How to tell: D lies beyond the present curve, with about the same M as A and more N. It can be reached only if the country's capacity to produce rises, and technological advancement is the option that raises capacity directly.

Why not the others:
A. reducing production: this moves the economy to a point inside the curve; it does not move the curve.
B. increasing saving: saving on its own adds no new resources, and it helps later only if the money is invested in new machines, so the syllabus does not treat it as the direct cause.
D. more farming: putting more resources into farming is a movement along the curve toward more of one good, not a shift of the whole curve.

Exam tip: a PPC shifts outward when a country gets more or better resources or better technology, such as new machines, a larger or better-trained workforce, or newly found resources. Anything that only changes the amount or the mix of output moves the point, not the curve.

items.hint1: Opportunity cost is about what you give up when you make a choice, not about what you spend on the thing you chose.
items.hint2: The government has two choices here. Once it picks the fuel subsidy, what does it no longer get? The money paid on the chosen option is its money cost, not its opportunity cost.
items.hint3: Two options describe the road that is given up. One describes it as the real thing people lose, the other as a sum of money. Which of these does economics use to state opportunity cost?
items.solution:
Answer: B. road left to decay

Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. In the syllabus it is stated as the real thing that is forgone, not as a sum of money.

How to tell: the government can either subsidise fuel or construct the road. Choosing the subsidy means the road work is not done, so the road is left to decay. That lost road is what the subsidy really costs the country.

Why not the others:
A. amount paid on subsidy: this is the money spent on the choice that was made, its money cost, not what was given up.
C. amount to be paid on road: it points to the road that was given up but states it as money, and in the syllabus opportunity cost is the real alternative forgone, not its money value.
D. none of the above: option B correctly names the alternative forgone.

Exam tip: to find an opportunity cost, name the choice that was made, then name the next best thing it pushed out. The answer is that thing itself, not the money spent on the choice made.

items.hint1: Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Here the demand equation is printed as Qr.
items.hint2: Set the two equations equal: 20 − ¼p = 5 + ½p. Then collect the p terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
items.hint3: Take 5 from both sides and add ¼p to both sides, so all the p terms are on the right. Work out ¼ + ½ and 20 − 5, then divide to find p.
items.solution:
Answer: D. #20

At the equilibrium price, the quantity buyers want (demand) equals the quantity sellers offer (supply), so there is no shortage and no surplus. With equations, you find it by setting demand equal to supply and solving for p. The # in the options stands for the naira sign, ₦, and Qr is the demand equation, Qd.

How to tell:
Qd = Qs
20 − ¼p = 5 + ½p
20 − 5 = ½p + ¼p
15 = ¾p
p = 15 × 4 ÷ 3
p = ₦20
Check: Qd = 20 − ¼ × 20 = 15 units and Qs = 5 + ½ × 20 = 15 units, so they match.

Why not the others:
A. #10: at ₦10, Qd = 17.5 units and Qs = 10 units, so demand is greater than supply.
B. #15: at ₦15, Qd = 16.25 units and Qs = 12.5 units, still not equal; 15 is the number on the left of 15 = ¾p, not p itself.
C. #18: at ₦18, Qd = 15.5 units and Qs = 14 units, still not equal.

Exam tip: to find equilibrium from equations, set Qd = Qs, solve for p, then put p back into both equations. If both give the same quantity, your price is right.

items.hint1: Equilibrium quantity is the amount bought and sold at the equilibrium price. Find the price first, then use it.
items.hint2: Put the equilibrium price into the demand equation, Q = 20 − ¼p. Then put it into the supply equation, Q = 5 + ½p, as a check. Both must give the same number.
items.hint3: Using p = 20, work out ¼ of 20 and take it away from 20. Be careful not to pick the price itself, which also appears among these options.
items.solution:
Answer: B. 15

The equilibrium quantity is the quantity at which demand and supply are equal. Once you know the equilibrium price, you put it into either equation, and both must give the same answer.

How to tell:
Equilibrium price, from the previous question: p = ₦20
Demand: Qd = 20 − ¼ × 20 = 20 − 5 = 15 units
Supply: Qs = 5 + ½ × 20 = 5 + 10 = 15 units
Both give 15 units, so the equilibrium quantity is 15 units.

Why not the others:
A. 10: this is only the ½p part of the supply equation at p = 20; the 5 still has to be added.
C. 18: neither equation gives 18 units at p = ₦20.
D. 20: this is the equilibrium price in naira, not the quantity; it is also the fixed number in the demand equation.

Exam tip: when one pair of equations carries both a price question and a quantity question, the price often turns up among the quantity options. Write the unit (₦ or units) beside every number you find so you do not mix them up.

items.hint1: Price elasticity of demand compares how strongly quantity demanded responds to a change in price. At one point on a demand equation you need two things: how much quantity changes for each ₦1 change in price, and the price divided by the quantity at that point.
items.hint2: From the demand equation Qd = 20 − ¼p, each ₦1 rise in price cuts quantity demanded by ¼ unit. The formula is: elasticity = (change in Q ÷ change in P) × (P ÷ Q), ignoring the minus sign.
items.hint3: Multiply the ¼ from the equation by P ÷ Q at this point, 4 ÷ 19, and simplify. Watch out: one option is the ¼ on its own, which leaves out the P ÷ Q part.
items.solution:
Answer: C. 1/19

Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price. At one point on a straight-line demand equation, it is the change in quantity for each ₦1 change in price, multiplied by the price divided by the quantity at that point. The minus sign is usually ignored, because quantity demanded falls as price rises.

How to tell:
Demand equation: Qd = 20 − ¼p
Each ₦1 rise in price lowers Qd by ¼ unit, so change in Q ÷ change in P = ¼ (ignoring the minus sign)
At the given point: P = ₦4 and Q = 19 units (check: 20 − ¼ × 4 = 20 − 1 = 19)
Elasticity = (change in Q ÷ change in P) × (P ÷ Q)
= ¼ × 4/19
= 4/76
= 1/19
The units cancel, so elasticity has no unit. Because 1/19 is less than 1, demand is inelastic at this point.

Why not the others:
A. 1/4: this is only the change in Q ÷ change in P from the equation; it leaves out P ÷ Q.
B. 1/2: this comes from the supply equation (½p), not the demand equation.
D. 1/20: this uses 20, the fixed number in the demand equation, in place of the quantity at this point, which is 19.

Exam tip: for point elasticity from a straight-line demand equation, take the number in front of p as the change in Q ÷ change in P, then multiply by P ÷ Q at the given point. If your answer equals the number in front of p alone, you have missed the second step.
